strengths: The paper addresses a relevant NLP evaluation problem: how collaborative workflows affect interactive qualitative coding. Comparing topic modeling, relational inference, and LLM-based labeling under a common framework is a useful contribution. :codex-file-citation{path="/fsx/homes/Yaochen.Wang@mbzuai.ac.ae/AI-reviewer/res/run-20260914-01/reviews/b02/review-experiment-hospet6d/call-51eb7a89441a40e68921d8e670a87ba7/manuscript.pdf" purpose="source"}
The study includes 15 coding sessions with 20 researchers on a shared corpus of approximately 85,000 tweets. Fixed initial partitions within each system reduce initialization variability.

The evaluation combines document overlap, semantic similarity, 1,200 manually checked document-theme pairs, and participant interviews. Double annotation with adjudication strengthens the manual evaluation. The paper also reports mixed outcomes, including greater cohesiveness without improved distinctiveness, and provides useful operational details and prompt templates.
weaknesses: The central comparison does not implement asynchronous collaboration as defined in the introduction. That definition includes independent work followed by consolidation, whereas Section 4 compares individual codebooks against codebooks produced by three-person synchronous teams, without consolidation. Synchrony is therefore confounded with team size and access to multiple perspectives. Participant allocation, reuse across the 27 participation slots, and time budgets are also unspecified. The evidence supports a narrower comparison between individual and group coding.

The statistical evidence is insufficiently justified. Each system has only two synchronous groups and three asynchronous coders, yielding just one synchronous codebook pair for consistency evaluation. Tables 1–2 report unpaired t-tests without identifying their observational units or sample sizes. Themes and comparisons sharing codebooks cannot simply be treated as independent replications of a collaboration condition. Analysis accounting for this dependence, uncertainty estimates, and potentially additional independent groups are needed to support the central significance claims; labeling results 'near statistically significant' does not resolve this.

Correctness is not reproducibly defined. Figure 4 reports F1, but Section 5 only describes judging assigned document-theme pairs, without defining recall, F1 aggregation, or pooling across runs. With 200 pairs per condition and Krippendorff’s alpha of 0.632, differences need uncertainty estimates. Table 4 reports 0.7–16.1% unlabeled LLM outputs, yet their treatment in correctness evaluation is unclear. Sampling weights and the treatment of unmapped relational outputs also require clarification.

The proposed consistency metrics need stronger validation. Maximum matching can reuse counterpart themes, while theme counts, sizes, and alignment symmetry are not reported. Consequently, codebook granularity can influence the scores. Centroid similarities near 0.98 coexist with much lower document overlap, illustrating why semantic similarity alone cannot establish equivalent codebooks. Granularity controls and human assessment of codebook quality would strengthen the framework’s interpretation.

Several conclusions exceed the tested configurations. One English vaccine-discussion dataset and one implementation per category cannot establish general properties of those model families. The relational system additionally uses domain-specific stance and morality information. Claims about LLM unreliability and expense rest on Llama 3.2 3B-Instruct; one supplied prompt even discusses software objects/classes and code functionality. Interaction bandwidth remains a plausible explanation rather than an experimentally isolated mechanism.

Reproducibility remains incomplete despite Section 9’s assurance. Missing details include the exact sentence-embedding checkpoint, resulting codebooks and per-run outputs, selected prompt for each LLM run, and decoding settings. Annotation results and analysis code are promised for future release but are not supplied through an accessible artifact in the manuscript. Together with the design and statistical ambiguities, these omissions prevent a clear Findings recommendation.

The interview findings are difficult to audit. Appendix C acknowledges missing interviews and different individual versus group interview formats, but gives neither completed interview counts nor a systematic analysis procedure. Comparative statements such as asynchronous coders being 'more likely' to notice tool inadequacies should therefore be presented as exploratory observations.
